pages.title: Unconstrained optimization: introduction
pages.body_text:
Consider the unconstrained optimization problem
min
z∈Rd ℓ(z),
with ℓ: Rd →R a cost function to be minimized and z a decision vector.
We say that z⋆is a
• global minimum if ℓ(z⋆) ≤ℓ(z) for all z ∈Rd
• strict global minimum if ℓ(z⋆) < ℓ(z) for all z̸ = z⋆
• local minimum if there exists ϵ > 0 such that ℓ(z⋆) ≤ℓ(z) for all
z ∈B(z⋆, ϵ) = {z ∈Rd | ∥z −z⋆∥< ϵ}
• strict local minimum if there exists ϵ > 0 such that ℓ(z⋆) < ℓ(z) for all z ∈B(z⋆, ϵ) and z̸ = z⋆.

pages.title: Necessary conditions of optimality (unconstrainted)
pages.body_text:
First order necessary condition (FNC) of optimality (unconstrained)
Let z⋆be an unconstrained local minimum of ℓ: Rd →R and assume that ℓis continuously differentiable
(C1) in B(z⋆, ϵ) for some ϵ > 0. Then ∇ℓ(z⋆) = 0.
Second order necessary condition of optimality (unconstrained)
If additionally ℓis twice continuously differentiable (C2) in B(z⋆, ϵ), then ∇2ℓ(z⋆) ≥0 (the Hessian
∇2ℓ(z⋆) of ℓis positive semidefinite).
Remark Points ¯z satisfying ∇ℓ(¯z) = 0 are called stationary points. They include minima, maxima and
saddle points.

pages.title: Minimization of convex functions
pages.body_text:
Proposition (Prop. B.10 Nonlin. Progr.)
Let Z ⊂Rd be a convex set and ℓ: Z →R a convex function. Then a local minimum of ℓis also a
global minimum.
Proof
Let z⋆be a local minimum of ℓ. Suppose by contradiction that z⋆is not a global minimum. Then there
exists a global minimum ¯z ∈X such that ℓ(¯z) < ℓ(z⋆).
Using the definition of convexity it holds
ℓ(θz⋆+ (1 −θ)¯z) ≤θℓ(z⋆) + (1 −θ)ℓ(¯z)
< θℓ(z⋆) + (1 −θ)ℓ(z⋆) = ℓ(z⋆),
for every θ ∈[0, 1).
This contradicts the assumption that z⋆is a local minimum since we found points, ˜z = θz⋆+ (1 −θ)¯z
with θ ∈[0, 1), arbitrarily close to z⋆with ℓ(˜z) < ℓ(z⋆). This concludes the proof.

pages.title: Minimization of convex functions
pages.body_text:
Necessary and sufficient condition of optimality (unconstrained)
For the unconstrained minimization of a convex function it can be shown that the first order necessary
condition of optimality is also sufficient (for a global minimum).
Proposition (Prop. 1.1.2 Nonlin. Progr.)
Let ℓ: Rd →R be a convex function. Then z⋆is a global minimum if and only if ∇ℓ(z⋆) = 0.
Proof (sketch)
Use the fact (Proposition B3 in Nonlinear Programming) that ℓconvex if and only if
ℓ(z) ≥ℓ(z⋆) + ∇ℓ(z⋆)T (z −z⋆)
for all z ∈Rd. Thus, if ∇ℓ(z⋆) = 0 it follows immediately ℓ(z) ≥ℓ(z⋆) for all z ∈Rd. The converse is
true by the first order necessary condition and the fact that a local minimum is a global minimum.

pages.body_text:
First-order necessary condition for optimality: if z⋆is a minimum then

Important
A necessary condition for the existence of minima for a quadratic program is that Q ≥0.
Thus, quadratic programs admitting at least a minimum are convex optimization problems.

The algorithm starts at a given initial guess z0 and iteratively generates vectors z1, z2, . . . such that ℓis

pages.title: Optimization algorithms: two-step procedure
pages.body_text:
We consider a general two-step procedure that reads as follows
zk+1 = zk + γkdk,
k = 1, 2, . . .
in which
1. each γk > 0 is a “step-size”,
2. dk ∈Rd is a “direction”.
The goal is to
1. choose a direction dk along which the cost decreases for γk sufficiently small;
2. select a step-size γk guaranteeing a sufficient decrease.
Notation In other references these are called line-search methods.

pages.title: Gradient methods: introduction
pages.body_text:
zk+1 = zk −γk∇ℓ(zk),
i.e., we choose dk = −∇ℓ(zk).
From the first order Taylor expansion of ℓat zk we have
ℓ(zk+1) = ℓ(zk) + ∇ℓ(zk)T (zk+1 −zk) + o(∥zk+1 −zk∥)
= ℓ(zk) −γk∥∇ℓ(zk)∥2 + o(γk).
Thus, for γk > 0 sufficiently small it can be shown that ℓ(zk+1) < ℓ(zk).

pages.title: Gradient methods: introduction

The update rule

pages.title: Gradient methods: convergence result (Armijo)
pages.body_text:
Proposition (convergence with Armijo step-size)
Let {zk} be a sequence generated by a gradient method zk+1 = zk−γkDk∇ℓ(zk) with d1I ≤Dk ≤d2I,
d1 > 0, d2 > 0. Assume that γk is chosen by the Armijo rule and ℓ(z) be continuously differentiable.
Then, every limit point ¯z of the sequence {zk} is a stationary point, i.e., ∇ℓ(¯z) = 0.
Remark Recall that a vector z ∈Rd is a limit point of a sequence {zk} in Rd if there exists a subsequence
of {zk} that converges to z.
